lead: Every thermodynamics problem starts by drawing a boundary. The system is what you choose to study; everything outside that can interact with it is the surroundings; the boundary is the surface, real or imaginary, fixed or moving, that separates them. What crosses the boundary decides the type of system: a closed system lets energy cross but no mass, an open system (control volume) lets both cross, and an isolated system lets neither. The same hardware, a pressure cooker or an LPG cylinder, can be any of these, depending on where you draw the line.
prereq: You need: the macroscopic view of a gas as a body with mass, volume and pressure.

blocks.text: Choose a fixed amount of matter or a region in space; that is the system. The boundary may be a real wall (the steel shell of a boiler drum), a moving surface (the face of a piston), or an imaginary surface drawn across a pipe where steam enters a turbine. Mass, heat and work are counted only where they cross this boundary, so the boundary must be drawn and labelled before any calculation.

A boundary is described by what it lets through. A diathermic wall lets heat pass; an adiabatic wall does not. A rigid wall cannot move, so no work is done by moving it, though a shaft or a wire can still carry work across it. A movable wall, like a piston face, lets displacement work cross.

Closed system (control mass). No mass crosses the boundary, so the mass inside is fixed. Heat and work may cross, and the boundary may move. Gas in a sealed piston–cylinder is the standard example: the piston can rise and the cylinder can be heated, but the same kilograms of gas stay inside.

Open system (control volume). Mass crosses the boundary, and energy may cross both as heat and work and carried by the moving mass. The boundary, called the control surface, is usually fixed around a device: a compressor, a steam turbine, a car radiator, a boiler. Some syllabi use the words open system and control volume for the same thing.

Isolated system. No mass, no heat and no work crosses. It is an ideal limit: a well-insulated, rigid, sealed flask comes close. The system and its surroundings taken together form an isolated system, an idea the second law uses later.

blocks.where: m₁ and m₂ are the masses inside at the start and end, in kg; mᵢ is the mass that enters and mₑ the mass that leaves during the period, in kg. A closed system has mᵢ = mₑ = 0, so m₂ = m₁.

sections.h3: Choosing the boundary, and steady running

blocks.text: The classification belongs to the boundary, not to the hardware. When air leaks from a tank, a boundary around the tank is crossed by mass, so that system is open. A boundary drawn around only the air that will stay in the tank is crossed by no mass at all, so that system is closed, but its boundary moves as the air expands to fill the tank. Both choices are correct; pick the one that makes the calculation easiest. Figure 1.2.1 shows the two choices for the worked example.

Open systems are usually analysed at steady state: at each fixed point inside the control volume, the properties do not change with time, and the mass inside stays constant because the inflow equals the outflow. A running turbine is steady while its inlet and outlet readings hold for hours. Steady state is not equilibrium; equilibrium has no flows and no gradients at all. Filling or emptying a tank is unsteady because the mass inside changes; the energy balance for both cases comes with the first law for control volumes.

figure.caption: The worked example’s rigid tank seen with two boundaries. Drawn around the tank (A), the boundary is fixed and 0.50 kg of air crosses it, so the system is open. Drawn around the 1.5 kg that stays (B), no mass crosses, so it is a closed system whose boundary moves.

examples.question: A rigid steel tank holds 2.0 kg of compressed air. A valve is opened until 0.50 kg of air has escaped, and during this time 30 kJ of heat leaves through the tank wall. (a) Take the tank (wall and valve opening) as the boundary: does mass cross, does energy cross, and what type of system is it? Find the final mass. (b) Now take as the system the air that is still in the tank at the end. What type of system is that? (c) Is either system isolated?
steps: (a) Boundary: the inner surface of the tank wall plus a surface across the valve opening. It is fixed in space.
Mass balance: m₂ = m₁ + mᵢ − mₑ = 2.0 + 0 − 0.50 = 1.5 kg. Since mₑ = 0.50 kg is not zero, mass crosses the boundary.

Energy crosses in two ways: 30 kJ of heat leaves through the wall, and the escaping 0.50 kg of air carries its own energy out through the valve. The tank is rigid, so no boundary work is done by its walls.
Mass crosses, so the tank is an open system, a control volume. Its boundary is fixed but its mass changes from 2.0 kg to 1.5 kg, so the process is unsteady.
(b) Boundary: a surface wrapped around the 1.5 kg of air that will remain. At the start this air fills three quarters of the tank (1.5 ÷ 2.0 = 0.75); at the end it fills the whole tank.

No air crosses this surface, so the mass stays 1.5 kg: a closed system, a control mass. Its boundary moves outward as the air expands and pushes the escaping air ahead of it, so this system does work on the escaping air.
(c) Neither system is isolated: heat leaves both, mass leaves the first and work leaves the second.
examples.answer: (a) Open (control volume), final mass 1.5 kg, with 0.50 kg and 30 kJ of heat crossing. (b) Closed (control mass) of 1.5 kg with a moving boundary. (c) Neither is isolated.

traps: Closed is not isolated. A closed system can exchange heat and work; only an isolated system blocks mass, heat and work.
Rigid does not mean adiabatic. A rigid steel tank still passes heat through its wall; rigid only rules out boundary work by the wall.
In an open system the mass that crosses also carries energy. When the 0.50 kg escapes, heat is not the only energy that leaves.
A sealed system is closed, not isolated, unless its wall is also adiabatic and no work crosses.
Steady state is not equilibrium: a steady turbine has flow and temperature differences inside, constant in time.

quiz.q: Define system, surroundings and boundary in one line each.
quiz.a: System: the matter or region chosen for study. Surroundings: everything outside it that can interact with it. Boundary: the real or imaginary surface between them.
A chosen region in space, usually around a device, across whose boundary (the control surface) mass and energy can flow: an open system.

quiz.q: Why can a closed system change its energy but not its mass?
quiz.a: By definition no mass crosses its boundary, so the mass is fixed. Heat and work can still cross, so its energy can rise or fall.

quiz.q: A turbine runs with constant inlet and outlet readings for hours. Is it in steady state, in equilibrium, or both?
quiz.a: Steady state only. Properties at each point are constant in time, but steam flows through and temperature and pressure differ from inlet to outlet, so it is not in equilibrium.

quiz.q: An LPG cylinder holds 14.2 kg of gas. A stove draws 0.25 kg in an evening, and no gas enters. Find the final mass and classify the cylinder as a system while the stove burns.
quiz.a: m₂ = 14.2 + 0 − 0.25 = 13.95 kg. Mass leaves through the valve, so the cylinder is an open system (control volume) during use.

quiz.q: A rigid tank holds 3.0 kg of air. A line adds 1.0 kg; no heat crosses and no shaft or electrical work is supplied. Take the tank as the system. Does mass cross? Is it isolated? Find the final mass.
quiz.a: Yes, 1.0 kg enters, so it is open, not isolated, even though Q = 0 and no shaft work is supplied; the entering air also carries energy in. m₂ = 3.0 + 1.0 − 0 = 4.0 kg.

quiz.q: A sealed steel flask of hot tea sits on a table. A student calls it an isolated system. Judge the claim.
quiz.a: Wrong. No mass crosses, so it is closed, but the steel wall is diathermic and the tea cools, so heat crosses. An isolated system would also need an adiabatic wall.

quiz.q: For a car tyre being inflated at a petrol pump, give one boundary that makes the system open and one that makes it closed.
quiz.a: Open: a fixed boundary around the tyre's inner volume, crossed by the incoming air at the valve. Closed: a boundary around all the air that will be in the tyre at the end, including the part still in the hose at the start; no mass crosses it, but it moves.

beyond: Engineers draw control volumes around a single turbine stage, a whole refrigerator or a data-centre cooling loop to write mass and energy balances. Computational fluid dynamics splits a flow into millions of tiny control volumes and balances each one. The formal link between a control mass and a control volume is the Reynolds transport theorem.
